 Systems administrators are among the first to point out lax security policies in other companies' or people's setups. Sometimes, they are the ones who get bitten by not taking the same advice they will so readily dispense. Such is the tale of Reddit user NakamuraHwang, who had files on their Synology DS918+ NAS encrypted by a ransomware attack after making a series of unforced errors.
 Hwang appears to be quite technically proficient and provided a detailed write-up of the situation. The key points, however, are that the unit in question (a) had its web interface exposed to the internet and (b) was roughly 18 months out-of-date with security patches. Just like the recent PHP snafu has adeptly shown , complacency is a far worse enemy than an army of AI bots.
 The tech has a 3-2-1 backup setup, so they seemingly didn't lose any data. They attached the disks to a Proxmox machine for further inspection — Synology's DSM operating system uses mdraid underneath , so you can take the disks to another box and mount them there. Investigation of logs and the operating system files revealed that the attack was likely performed by abusing the CVE-2024-10441 remote code execution vulnerability, revealed a year and a half ago.
 Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware 
 Watch full video here: 
 As most any other sysadmin will tell you, it's never advisable to expose devices directly to the internet without some layer of protection in between, chiefly but not only a VPN or an SSH tunnel. Tailscale, for instance, makes having a VPN fairly painless these days, and its free plan covers most home installations.
 Synology had published its own advisory regarding the exploit, but that's where the NAS' behavior regarding updates complicates matters. According to multiple comments on the thread and in other forums , the UI will happily tell you that your device is up to date, all while there are critical security updates that need to be manually installed. The manual for DSM indicates that units from 2025 onwards have automatic updates, apparently implying that those of previous makes need to be configured so.

 A first file box (NAS) for one person
 You can share files from the old laptop for a while. A NAS is the later box: a quiet machine with hard drives that keeps photos and backups in one place. Two drive bays and simple software if you just want backups that restore. More bays and a faster port if you already know you will run extra apps on it.
 Start at what you already have if you don't have a file box yet. A USB drive on the old laptop is enough to learn. The empty NAS is the teaser price. The drives are the real bill. Budget NAS-rated 4–8 TB disks on top, then a spare. Anyone quoting a NAS without drive math is selling a chassis.
 What to buy
 Box Why Street, 2026 Skip if 
 Synology DS223 (Value 2-bay) DSM and sleep without Plus packages. 2 GB soldered, one 1GbE. Skip the j. Diskless often $250–285. Confirm B0BRNBVTJK, not a drive kit. You need Container Manager, a RAM lid, or dual LAN. That is DS224+.

Best Budget NAS and Cheapest NAS Setups for 2026 | Starry Hope Starry Hope 
 The Best Budget NAS in 2026, Priced With Two Drives
Updated on
 November 2, 2026,
by Jim Mendenhall 
 Bottom line 
 The UGREEN DXP2800 is our budget NAS pick for most homes that want Plex, photo backup, and a few apps. It costs a little more than the cheapest two-bay boxes, and it adds two SSD slots and a faster network port. A household that only needs backups can save money with the cheaper UGREEN DH2300.
Recommendation
 Pair the DXP2800 with two 8TB NAS drives if the budget allows, since two 4TB drives cost less but fill up sooner.
 The UGREEN DXP2800 is our pick for most homes on a budget, and with two NAS hard drives the whole setup costs about $770 to $1,110. Two drives are the smallest setup that survives a drive failure, so every total below includes them. Hard drive prices roughly doubled over the past two years, and a pair of 4TB NAS drives now costs about as much as the DXP2800 itself. That shrinks what the cheaper boxes save. The DXP2800 adds $120 to $150 to the total over the cheapest two-bay setup, and the money buys a faster network port, an Intel chip that transcodes video, and two SSD slots.
 Every price below is a maker’s list or store price for the box, plus a rounded range for the drives as of October 2026. Drive prices move by tens of dollars from week to week.
 What the cheapest NAS setups cost with two drives
 The table pairs each box with two 4TB NAS drives (about $380 to $480 for the pair) and two 8TB NAS drives (about $660 to $720). In RAID 1, the mirror layout for two drives, two 4TB drives give you 4TB of usable space and two 8TB drives give you 8TB, because every file is written to both drives.
 Box Bays Box price With two 4TB drives With two 8TB drives 
 UGREEN DH2300 2 $269.99 list, $239.99 on sale about $620 to $750 about $900 to $990 
 TerraMaster F2-425 2 $299.99 list, $254.99 on sale about $635 to $780 about $915 to $1,020 
 UGREEN DXP2800 2 $389.99 (marked down from $439.99) about $770 to $870 about $1,050 to $1,110 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus (N95) 4 $599.99 about $980 to $1,080 about $1,260 to $1,320 
 UGREEN DXP4800 GT 4 $659.99 about $1,040 to $1,140 about $1,320 to $1,380 
 The lowest total on the list is about $620, and that buys 4TB of mirrored storage on a box with a 1GbE port, 4GB of fixed RAM, and no official Docker support. The DXP2800 setup costs about $120 to $150 more and gives the same 4TB with a 2.5GbE port, a chip that runs Plex and Docker, and two M.2 SSD slots. With 8TB drives the gap between those two setups stays the same in dollars and shrinks as a share of the total.
 The two four-bay boxes in the table cost $210 to $270 more than the DXP2800 and do not need all four drives on day one. Two drives in a four-bay box leave two empty bays for later, which matters more now that the cheapest way to add space is to add a drive rather than replace both.
 Our budget pick is the UGREEN DXP2800
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800
 Editor's Choice 
 2-Bay 2.5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N100 
 List price $389.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The UGREEN DXP2800 costs $389.99 on UGREEN’s store, marked down from $439.99, and runs on an Intel N100, a four-core chip from 2023 with Intel Quick Sync, the video engine that lets Plex or Jellyfin convert a 4K movie for a phone or an older TV without loading the CPU. It ships with 8GB of DDR5 in one slot (16GB maximum), a 2.5GbE port, two M.2 NVMe slots, and tool-less 3.5-inch trays in a metal case. A 2.5GbE port moves about 280 MB/s, close to the 300 MB/s that TechRadar gives as the practical ceiling for two hard drives striped together. A 1GbE port tops out near 115 MB/s.
 UGREEN’s UGOS Pro software includes a Docker app, so Immich, Home Assistant, or Pi-hole can run next to the file shares. The M.2 slots take an SSD cache or a separate SSD pool for those apps. UGREEN also lets you install TrueNAS or Unraid without voiding the warranty, so you can switch systems later without buying new hardware. OCinside measured about 7 W at idle in its December 2024 review , so the box itself costs about $10 a year to run at 17 cents per kWh; two spinning drives add more, and our 24/7 power cost math covers how to price that at your local rate.
 Two bays mean RAID 1 or RAID 0 only, so growing past two drives means replacing both with larger ones. There is no PCIe slot, so the only route past 2.5GbE is a USB network adapter. UGOS Pro has fewer apps than Synology’s DSM, and Plex and Jellyfin install as Docker containers rather than one-click packages. How-To Geek’s review of a pre-release unit in April 2024 said UGOS “needs a lot of work”; Docker and most of the missing features arrived in later updates, and Macworld’s July 2025 review called the interface intuitive but found UGOS Pro less mature than Synology’s and QNAP’s systems.
 The UGREEN DH2300 is the cheapest box and suits backups only
 The UGREEN DH2300 launched in 2025 at $209.99, and in October 2026 UGREEN’s store lists it at $269.99, on sale for $239.99. It runs UGOS Pro on a Rockchip RK3576, an eight-core ARM chip, with 4GB of RAM soldered to the board and a single 1GbE port. TechRadar’s November 2025 review by Mark Pickavance gave it 4.5 out of 5 and called it “a terrific NAS that does most of what these things are bought for, without breaking the bank.”
 It handles phone photo backup, a shared folder, and nightly PC backups. TechRadar measured 118 MB/s over the built-in 1GbE port with two 4TB IronWolf drives. With a USB 2.5GbE adapter (about $25), reads rose to 296 MB/s and writes to 286 MB/s. TechRadar also found that a cheap SATA SSD can act as a read cache for a single hard drive.
 The RAM cannot be upgraded, and UGREEN’s product page says the DH2300 does not have official Docker support or virtual machines. TechRadar wrote that with 4GB “it can only handle a couple of major Docker containers.” The ARM chip cannot run Windows or Linux virtual machines, and there are no M.2 slots. Even with a $25 USB 2.5GbE adapter, the DH2300 setup costs about $95 to $125 less than a DXP2800 setup, about 11% to 16% of the DXP2800 setup’s total with 4TB drives.
 The TerraMaster F2-425 is the cheapest Intel two-bay
 The TerraMaster F2-425 sits between the two UGREEN boxes. It pairs an Intel Celeron N5095 from 2021 with 4GB of DDR4 (16GB maximum), a 2.5GbE port, and TerraMaster’s TOS software, and TerraMaster’s store lists it at $299.99 with sales to about $255. Because it is an Intel chip, it runs Docker and virtual machines and has Quick Sync for video transcoding. PCWorld’s October 2025 review by Jon L. Jacobi called it “a good value for streaming media over your home network, handling IP cams, and backing up your computer,” and listed “occasional interface rough spots” and an “all-plastic case” as its cons.
 It has no M.2 slots, and its chip is two years older than the N100 in the DXP2800. At sale prices it is about $135 below the DXP2800. That buys Plex and a couple of containers if you can do without SSD slots. At its $299.99 list price the gap to the DXP2800 shrinks to $90, and the DXP2800 is the better use of that money.
 Four-bay boxes leave room for two more drives
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 Most Expandable 
 4-Bay 5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N95 
 List price $599.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 GT
 Best Performance 
 4-Bay 10GbE 8GB RAM AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 
 List price $659.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 A two-bay NAS has one upgrade path: replace both drives with larger ones and copy the data across. A four-bay box lets you start with two drives in RAID 1 and add two more later, or move to RAID 5, where one drive’s worth of space protects the rest. If your photo and video library keeps growing, adding drives to empty bays avoids retiring a working pair of drives. Our NAS comparison chart treats four bays as the practical starting point for a home NAS, and that holds for anyone who can see past 8TB. On a tight budget, a two-bay box is the cheaper entry.
 Close modal 
 The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus in its Intel N95 version lists at $599.99 with 8GB of DDR4, three M.2 NVMe slots, and two 5GbE ports, which is faster networking than any other box in this guide except the DXP4800 GT. The N95 is a 2023 chip in the same class as the DXP2800’s N100, with Quick Sync. The cons are a single RAM slot, M.2 slots that each run at one PCIe lane, and no PCIe slot for a 10GbE card.
 The UGREEN DXP4800 GT lists at $659.99 and moves to an AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 with two 10GbE ports and ECC memory support. It is the only box here with 10GbE, which only pays off if your PC and switch also have 10GbE. It transcodes H.264 and H.265 video, but PCWorld’s review measured about 25 W with the drives asleep, so it costs more to run around the clock than the Intel N-series boxes.
 For tinkerers there is also the AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U , a four-bay barebone at $379 with an eight-core Ryzen 7 5825U and dual 2.5GbE. It ships with no RAM, no SSD, and no NAS software, so the full cost is $379 plus a DDR4 kit and a boot SSD, plus an evening installing TrueNAS or Unraid. The bays are not hot-swappable, so you power it down to change a drive. It is a poor fit for anyone who wants a setup wizard.
 Drive prices doubled, and small drives cost the most per terabyte
 Close modal 
 The NASDisks price tracker reports that the typical NAS hard drive of 8TB and up went from $21 per terabyte in July 2024 to $47 per terabyte in October 2026, more than double. MakeUseOf’s September 2026 report traces the cause to data center demand: “Western Digital says it’s sold out of nearline hard drive capacity through calendar 2026.” Analysts cited in that report do not expect prices to normalize before late 2027, so waiting for a sale is a weak plan.
 At the cheaper end of each size, a 4TB NAS drive costs roughly $48 to $60 per terabyte, an 8TB drive about $41 to $45, and 12TB drives fall to about $36. The 4TB pair is still the lowest total outlay. If you can spend about $250 more, the 8TB pair doubles your usable space for about 60% more on the drives.
 The drives to look for are CMR models sold for NAS use, such as WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf, or Toshiba N300. CMR (conventional magnetic recording) drives handle the long rebuild a RAID mirror runs after a drive swap. Plain WD Red drives (without “Plus”) in the 2TB to 6TB range use SMR (shingled magnetic recording), which writes slowly under sustained load and can stretch a rebuild into days. Recertified enterprise drives were the budget trick of 2024 and 2025, and they no longer help much. PC Server and Parts tracked a recertified 24TB Seagate Exos going from $298.99 to $699 in a year.
 SSD prices rose too. NASCompares’ July 2026 roundup shows 4TB NVMe SSDs that sold for about $190 to $230 in June 2025 listed at about $699 to $900 or more. At those prices, an all-SSD NAS costs far more per terabyte than one with hard drives.
 Where Synology and a mini PC fit
 Synology’s cheapest two-bay, the DS223j, runs Synology’s DSM software on a Realtek RTD1619B with 1GB of RAM and a 1GbE port. When TechRadar reviewed the DH2300 at its $209.99 launch price, it noted the DS223j cost “a few dollars less” and had a weaker chip and a quarter of the memory. Its draw is DSM’s backup apps, such as Hyper Backup and Snapshot Replication. Synology’s two-bay DS225+ starts near $400, the same price as a DXP2800, with a 2019 Celeron and 2GB of RAM; see our UGREEN vs Synology comparison for that matchup.
 A used office mini PC with TrueNAS or Unraid is cheaper still for the box: off-lease Dell OptiPlex and Lenovo ThinkCentre Micro models sell for $100 to $200. They hold one or two internal drives, have 1GbE, and need a USB enclosure for more disks, which is a weaker setup for a RAID mirror than a NAS with dedicated drive bays. Our guide to using a mini PC as a NAS covers that route, including the Beelink ME Mini , a small box with six M.2 SSD slots. The ME Mini was a cheap NAS in 2025, but with 4TB SSDs now costing several times a 4TB hard drive, it has become a pricey way to buy capacity.
 Which budget setup to buy
 For most homes, the setup we would choose is the UGREEN DXP2800 with two 8TB NAS drives, at roughly $1,050 to $1,110. If that is too much, two 4TB drives bring the total down to roughly $770 to $870 and still give you a working mirror. Nothing cheaper in this guide pairs Quick Sync video transcoding and Docker with SSD slots and a 2.5GbE port.
 Someone who only wants a home for backups and shared files can spend less. The UGREEN DH2300 with two 4TB drives comes to about $620 to $750, and a $25 USB 2.5GbE adapter is worth adding if your PC has a 2.5GbE port. If your files could outgrow 8TB within a few years, the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus N95 model with two drives makes more sense, because adding two drives later costs less than replacing both drives in a two-bay box.
 Whatever you buy, a RAID 1 mirror protects you from a dead drive, not from a deleted folder, ransomware, or a house fire. Keep a second copy of the files you cannot replace on a USB drive or a cloud backup service.  Why this NAS and tier win
 DS223 is not the fastest two-bay NAS, which is precisely why it belongs in the entry backup tier. Its fixed 2GB memory and 1GbE port are adequate for scheduled computer backup, phone uploads, file history, and restores. TechRadar reached the same basic trade-off: DSM and low operating complexity are the strengths, while raw hardware value and small-file performance are the compromises. [ 1 ] [ 2 ] 
 The recommendation is based on the backup stack rather than RAID alone. Hyper Backup can create versioned copies to USB, another NAS, or supported cloud destinations. A mirror helps the system stay available after one disk fails, but it cannot recover files after theft, fire, enclosure failure, or every ransomware event. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] 
 Why these exact drives
 The exact ST4000VN006 is a current 4TB CMR IronWolf model in the catalog. Two disks create a simple mirror with 4TB decimal usable before formatting. This capacity is intentionally modest: it keeps the entry total controlled and makes the recommendation honest for documents, photos, and ordinary household-device backups. [ 5 ] 
 A measured 4TB comparison found that family labels alone do not settle noise, power, or value. The selected IronWolf is therefore an exact MPN, not a generic promise that every IronWolf is quieter or more reliable than every WD Red. [ 6 ] 
 Capacity and protection plan
 2 equal 4 TB drives with 1 drive-equivalent reserved for redundancy produce an editorial planning estimate of 4 TB decimal usable before formatting, filesystem metadata, snapshots, applications, and free-space reserve.
 The mirror can continue after one drive fails; RAID is not a backup. Reconfirm the RAID/SHR/RAIDZ behavior for the exact operating system and chosen disk layout before initialization.
 What YouTube and community evidence change
 In Synology community comparisons, DS223 is repeatedly treated as sufficient for backup and file storage, while DS225+ is recommended when 2.5GbE, containers, or longer performance headroom justify the extra cost. That is a useful boundary: entry should not quietly become a midrange purchase. [ 7 ] 
 Backup-focused YouTube guidance consistently separates snapshots, synchronization, and a second backup destination. The popular SpaceRex overview is commercially affiliated but useful because it compares the workflows instead of claiming that one RAID array is complete protection. [ 4 ] 
 Trade-offs before buying
 Both bays are occupied, so capacity growth requires replacing both drives. 
 1GbE is slower for large restores than 2.5GbE, although ordinary scheduled backups often run unattended. 
 Fixed memory and ARM-class software compatibility make this a poor choice for a growing container or media-transcoding plan. 
 Recommended setup sequence
 1 Measure current data across every computer, phone, and loose external drive. 
 2 Create an SHR/RAID1-style mirror and enable Btrfs snapshots for protected shares. 
 3 Assign each computer its own backup job and quota rather than copying files manually. 
 4 Add a versioned USB or encrypted off-site target before calling the system complete. 
 5 Run a test restore, record the steps, and repeat the test at least quarterly. 
 Alternatives worth considering
 Move up to DS225+ for 2.5GbE DS225+ Worth the extra cost when large restores, phone-photo indexing, or light containers are already part of the plan.
 Choose ASUSTOR for lower hardware cost AS1202T Faster networking and good value, but the independent consensus around beginner backup administration is weaker than DSM.
 Frequently asked questions
 Is 4TB enough for home backup? It is enough when current protected data is well below 3TB and growth is moderate. Add every device, include version history, reserve about 20%, and choose a larger tier if the result is close to 4TB.
 Does RAID1 mean the files are backed up? No. RAID1 keeps the NAS available after one disk fails. It mirrors deletion, corruption, and many ransomware changes, so an independent versioned copy is still required.
 Should I buy DS225+ instead of DS223? Choose DS225+ when 2.5GbE, Synology Photos indexing, or light Docker app hosting is already planned. For scheduled household computer backups alone, DS223 keeps the entry budget focused without paying for unused compute.
 Can I mix different hard drive brands or capacities in DS223? Under Synology SHR, you can mix capacities later, but in a 2-bay mirror, the total usable storage is strictly limited to the capacity of the smallest drive.

 If your only goal is to protect one laptop and you do not need local shared storage, an established cloud backup service plus a periodic external-drive copy may be simpler and cheaper to operate. A NAS becomes useful when several devices need a common local destination, fast restores, file sharing, or control over where the main copy lives. A mirrored or redundant NAS is still one copy in one location; it is not a complete backup. 
 Our practical default is two compatible NAS HDDs in a mirrored 2-bay system , a UPS, and a separate versioned off-site copy.  Work out the real capacity and cost
 First measure the data to protect: computers, shared folders, photos, and any large project files. Add expected growth and room for file versions; do not size the pool to 100% of today's data. Then choose the failure tolerance and confirm the layout in the vendor's RAID calculator.
 For example, two 8TB drives mirrored yield about 8TB nominal usable before filesystem and system overhead. Four 8TB drives with one-drive redundancy yield about 24TB nominal usable before overhead, depending on the chosen layout. Operating systems often display capacities in tebibytes (TiB), so a displayed number will be smaller than the decimal TB figure on the box. Redundancy lets a pool survive a specified drive failure; it does not undo deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or a failed backup job.
 Make a purchase worksheet with these lines:
 Diskless enclosure and drives: check model, drive capacity, quantity, and whether the seller bundled drives you did not choose. Use drives intended for NAS operation and check the exact model and firmware against the vendor's current compatibility list.
 One spare or replacement plan: decide how quickly a failed drive can be replaced and who will handle the rebuild. A spare in a drawer is optional for a home and more valuable when downtime is costly.
 UPS and network path: protect the NAS, switch, router, and internet handoff as needed. Size runtime from actual wattage; a 1500VA label is not a runtime promise. Connect the UPS to the NAS for supported graceful shutdown behavior.
 Off-site copy: price a second location, external drive rotation, or cloud object-storage plan. Include monthly storage, retrieval, and internet upload costs where relevant.
 Time and subscriptions: allow for setup, monitoring, restore exercises, and any destination or application fees. Confirm current package and service terms before committing to a workflow.
 For a straightforward Synology pair, the HAT3320-8T appears in the DS225+ product page's compatible accessories and on the DS925+ compatibility page . Reconfirm the exact model and firmware on the current compatibility list immediately before ordering. Under DSM 7.3's policy , 2025 DiskStation Plus systems can create pools using nonvalidated third-party HDDs and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs, but Synology limits support for issues caused by the drive or firmware.  Build a backup you can restore
 Use the NAS as a local destination, then protect the NAS itself. This is a practical starting workflow, which you should adapt to your devices and retention needs:
 Decide what must return first. List critical folders, computer images where needed, account owners, and acceptable recovery time. Exclude replaceable caches, but include the NAS configuration and any application data needed to rebuild the service.
 Automate client backups. Configure each computer or server to back up to a dedicated NAS share using a supported client tool. Set schedules and version retention. A shared folder that users manually copy into is useful for collaboration but is not a dependable client backup on its own.
 Back up the NAS off-site. On Synology, configure Hyper Backup to a supported second NAS, cloud destination, or rotated external drive. On UGREEN, use Sync & Backup for an incremental external or remote copy; check whether the selected cloud workflow retains older versions rather than simply synchronizing changes and deletions. On QNAP, check the current HBS 3 destination and versioning options. Give every brand's off-site copy separate credentials and test its restore path before relying on it.
 Watch every job. Set email or app alerts for failed backups, degraded storage, capacity, and UPS events. Give one person ownership of the alerts and replacement process. Record the job schedule and where credentials and recovery keys are stored.
 Prove recovery. Each month, restore a recent file and an older version to a separate location and open them. Periodically test a full computer or critical share restore, including the off-site copy, and note the time taken. Synology documents Hyper Backup restores ; UGREEN's backup strategy explains the different recovery behavior of snapshots, incremental copies, and mirrors. A successful job notification alone does not prove usable recovery.
 This follows the 3-2-1 principle described by CISA : three copies, two media or storage types, and one off-site. For a small office, consider an offline or immutable copy as extra protection against account compromise. Set retention and access rules from the actual business need, not a generic preset.
 Remote access and maintenance
 Keep the NAS management interface off the open internet. Use a maintained VPN or the vendor's supported secure remote-access method, enable multi-factor authentication where available, remove unused accounts, and keep NAS packages and clients updated. Give staff only the shares they need. For confidential files, check encryption at rest and in transit, and document where recovery keys live. These choices matter as much as the brand of enclosure.
 Review capacity and backup alerts weekly, apply security updates on a planned schedule, and replace a failed drive promptly. After any drive replacement, let the pool finish its rebuild and verify backup jobs again. If camera recording is the main workload, use our separate NVR vs NAS vs cloud camera-storage guide ; camera retention and surveillance licensing need their own sizing exercise.
 Buying links and seller check
 The UGREEN cards use tracked links to the matching model pages on UGREEN's US store. Their offers are sold by UGREEN; check the selected variant, included drives, current return terms, and final checkout details before ordering. Each enclosure discussed here is priced and described as diskless unless a particular store offer explicitly says otherwise.

The HAT3320-8T offer showed Adorama as shipper and seller; its card selects that merchant's offer. Adorama's seller profile showed 4.5/5 stars, 88% positive feedback over the previous 12 months, and 2,559 recent ratings when checked for the related UniFi buying guide. That is a known electronics retailer, but its recent feedback calls for a careful review of the actual offer. Amazon offers can change. Before checkout, confirm the model and capacity, new condition, shipper, seller, current feedback, returns, and warranty. Product star ratings alone do not establish seller reliability.

 FAQs
 Is RAID a backup?
 No. RAID or mirroring can keep the NAS running after a supported drive failure. It cannot recover data deleted or encrypted on the same system if all accessible versions are affected. Keep another versioned copy, preferably off-site, and test restoring it.
 Is a 2-bay NAS enough for a small office?
 It can be if current data, version retention, and growth fit a mirrored pair and restore time is acceptable. If several users create large files or capacity will grow quickly, price a 4-bay system before buying two larger drives for the smaller box.
 Should I use a NAS instead of cloud backup?
 They solve different parts of the problem. The NAS gives local storage and quick local restores; off-site cloud or a second location protects against loss of the local site. A single-device household without shared storage may be better served by cloud backup and an external copy.

 A NAS is the most reliable way to implement 3-2-1 backup at home — three copies of your data, two local on different media, one offsite. The right NAS makes this nearly automatic.
 Most people's backup strategy is either nonexistent or dangerously incomplete — a single external hard drive that hasn't been plugged in for six months, or cloud storage that covers photos but nothing else. A NAS changes this by becoming an always-on, always-connected backup target that your computers, phones, and tablets back up to automatically, every day, without any manual intervention.
 The right backup NAS for home and small office use needs three things: reliable backup software that handles versioning and scheduling, broad compatibility with Mac Time Machine and Windows backup, and a path to offsite backup for the copy that lives outside your home. Synology's DSM software leads the field on all three counts, which is why Synology appears prominently in these recommendations — but QNAP and others are competitive for users who want alternatives.

 The 3-2-1 Backup Rule: Why One Copy Is Never Enough
 The 3-2-1 backup rule is the most widely accepted framework for data protection, and for good reason: it addresses the most common failure modes simultaneously. The rule is simple: keep three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with one copy stored offsite.
 In a home context, this typically looks like: copy one is the original data on your computer's internal drive; copy two is the local backup on your NAS; copy three is an offsite backup in the cloud or on a drive stored at a different physical location. The two-media requirement ensures that a single failure event — a power surge, a fire, a ransomware attack — cannot take out both local copies at once. The offsite requirement ensures that a physical disaster at your home cannot destroy all your copies.
 A NAS is the natural home for copy two. It sits on your network, backs up your computers automatically, stores multiple versions so you can recover accidentally deleted files, and serves as the staging point for sending copy three to the cloud. A NAS alone is not the complete solution — it is one-third of it — but without a NAS, most people never reliably implement copies two and three at all.
 For small offices, the same logic applies at larger scale: a NAS backs up workstations and servers on the local network, while Hyper Backup or Hybrid Backup Sync pushes encrypted copies to cloud storage on a schedule. This gives you fast local restores for the common case (a user deleted an important file) and offsite recovery for the disaster case (the office burns down).
 RAID Is Not a Backup: What RAID Protects Against and What It Doesn't
 This point deserves its own section because it is the most common misconception about NAS backup. RAID — whether RAID 1 mirroring or RAID 5 parity — is a drive failure tolerance mechanism, not a backup. It is an important feature for keeping a NAS running after a drive fails, but it does not protect your data in most scenarios that actually cause data loss.
 RAID 1 keeps two identical copies of your data across two drives. If one drive fails, the NAS keeps running on the surviving drive. This is valuable — it means a drive failure doesn't result in downtime or data loss and gives you time to replace the failed drive. What RAID does not protect against: accidental file deletion (deletes are mirrored instantly to both drives), ransomware (encryption propagates to all drives in real time), the NAS enclosure failing (both drives survive but may not be readable elsewhere), theft (an attacker takes both drives), fire or flood (destroys both drives simultaneously).
 Run RAID 1 on your backup NAS — absolutely. It reduces the risk that a single drive failure takes your backup target offline at the worst possible moment. But run RAID in addition to proper backups, never instead of them.
 Synology Hyper Backup: Setting Up Versioned Backup With Retention Policies
 Hyper Backup is Synology's flagship backup application and one of the most capable backup tools available on any NAS platform. It backs up data from the NAS to external destinations — USB drives, rsync servers, or cloud storage — with full versioning, deduplication, and flexible retention policies.
 The versioning model is particularly useful: Hyper Backup stores incremental snapshots on a configurable schedule, and you can configure how many versions to retain and how far back they go. A typical home policy might keep daily backups for 30 days, weekly backups for 6 months, and monthly backups for 2 years. This lets you recover a file you deleted a year ago, not just last week.
 Deduplication means Hyper Backup is storage-efficient: if a file doesn't change between backup runs, only one copy is stored, with additional versions referencing it. This keeps offsite cloud storage costs manageable even with deep version history.
 Critically: test your restores. A backup you have never tested is a backup of unknown reliability. Hyper Backup includes a restore integrity check function — run it monthly to verify your backup is readable. Actually restore a few files periodically to confirm the process works end to end.
 Mac Time Machine and Windows Backup to a NAS
 Every Synology, QNAP, and TerraMaster NAS supports Time Machine over SMB, making them drop-in Time Machine targets for Mac users. The setup process on Synology is straightforward: create a dedicated shared folder for Time Machine backups in DSM, enable it as a Time Machine destination (DSM has a dedicated toggle for this), and set a storage quota so Time Machine doesn't consume the entire volume. On the Mac side, open Time Machine preferences, click Add Backup Disk, and your NAS folder appears in the list.
 One important detail: set a Time Machine quota on the NAS. Without a quota, Time Machine will eventually fill your entire NAS volume. A quota of 1.5–2x the Mac's internal storage capacity is usually appropriate, giving Time Machine room for multiple version snapshots while preserving space for other uses.
 For Windows, File History is the built-in backup tool and works well with a NAS SMB share as the backup destination. Navigate to Settings > Update & Security > Backup, point it at a NAS network share, and Windows backs up your files on a schedule. Windows Server Backup and Veeam Agent for Windows (which has a free tier) offer more advanced options including full system image backups, useful for small offices that need bare-metal restore capability.
 Offsite Backup from a NAS: Cloud Sync Options
 The offsite copy is the one most people skip, and it is the one that matters most when disaster strikes. Synology Hyper Backup and QNAP Hybrid Backup Sync both support sending encrypted backups directly to cloud storage on a schedule, making offsite backup as close to automatic as possible.
 Backblaze B2 is the most cost-effective option for most users at $0.006 per GB per month — 1 TB of offsite backup costs about $6/month, 5 TB costs $30/month. Amazon S3 is more expensive but widely supported. Google Drive and OneDrive are options if you already have storage there, though they cost more per GB than dedicated object storage.
 Encryption before upload is essential. Both Hyper Backup and Hybrid Backup Sync encrypt data with your own key before it leaves your NAS. This means the cloud provider cannot read your files, and a breach of the cloud provider doesn't expose your data. Keep your encryption key stored safely somewhere other than the NAS itself — losing the key means losing access to your offsite backup.
 For the initial upload of large data sets, be realistic about timing. A 1 TB initial backup upload over a 100 Mbps upload connection takes roughly 22 hours. A 5 TB initial upload takes 4–5 days. Plan to run the initial backup over several days in the background, then let incremental daily backups keep it current — incremental uploads of the day's changes are typically a few GB and complete overnight.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Does a NAS replace cloud backup?
 No. A NAS is the local component of a 3-2-1 backup strategy, not a replacement for offsite backup. A NAS and cloud backup are complementary: the NAS gives you fast local restores and versioning, while cloud backup protects against fire, flood, theft, and other physical disasters that could destroy both your computer and your NAS simultaneously.
 Can I use a NAS as a Time Machine backup target?
 Yes. Synology, QNAP, TerraMaster, and most NAS devices support Time Machine over SMB. Synology DSM makes Time Machine setup particularly easy — create a shared folder, enable it as a Time Machine destination in DSM, and the Mac finds it automatically in Time Machine preferences. Set a storage quota so Time Machine does not consume the entire NAS volume.
 How much storage do I need for a backup NAS?
 A good starting point is 2–3x the total size of the data you want to protect, to allow for multiple backup versions and retention history. If you are backing up a 1 TB laptop and a 500 GB desktop, plan for 3–5 TB of usable NAS storage. In a 2-bay RAID 1 configuration, that means two 4–6 TB drives.
 What happens if my NAS dies and I have all my backups on it?
 This is exactly why RAID alone is not a backup strategy, and why the 3-2-1 rule requires at least one copy offsite. If the NAS is destroyed by fire, flood, theft, or a power surge, all data on it is gone regardless of RAID configuration. Always keep at least one copy of your critical data somewhere physically separate from your NAS — a cloud service like Backblaze B2, an external drive stored at another location, or both.

 For the DXP4800 Plus, move to 10GbE when the client, switch and storage can all use it. Our DAC vs RJ45 vs fibre guide covers that next step. Two network ports do not automatically double one file transfer’s speed.
 To connect a desktop or server to that faster NAS, use our 10GbE NIC guide : match a copper card to the DXP4800 Plus, or choose SFP+ for a compatible switch uplink.

 Make an offsite backup and restore a file. Hyper Backup supplies Synology’s versioned destination options. Pick the equivalent supported backup route on UGOS and verify that you can recover your data.
 Add a UPS and test shutdown. Use our NAS-friendly UPS guide to match the USB/NUT route, then test a controlled power-loss shutdown before you need it.
 When DIY is the better answer
 Build your own when you want more drive bays, a specific expansion card or full control over the storage OS. Start with the SATA/HBA guide , NAS drives and ZFS vs mdadm vs hardware RAID . Choose the case, cooling and power supply around those parts.
 Prefer an appliance? DXP2800 starts the media server, DXP4800 Plus grows it to four bays, and DS225+ or DS925+ gives you DSM at the size you need. Pick the box, give your backups somewhere else to live, and get back to the fun projects.
